title: Every child's answer
hook: the Haggadah's four children come from midrash: each owed their own answer
tomorrow: after forty days of midrash, is there room left for your question?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pharaoh's daughter took in a child who wasn't hers, and the midrash named her Bityah, daughter of God. Today, more children, and the question of what each one is owed.
screen: `DAUGHTER OF GOD.` → `WHAT EACH CHILD IS OWED.`

segments.voice: Try explaining the same hard news to a five-year-old, a twelve-year-old and a skeptical sixteen-year-old. It's three different conversations. Same facts, three sizes, and one of them might roll their eyes at you. The rabbis noticed the Torah does this too, and from it came the four children at the seder table.
screen: `SAME NEWS, THREE AGES.` → `THREE CONVERSATIONS.` → `THE FOUR CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: The Torah has four separate places where a child asks, or is told, about leaving Egypt, and the verses don't match. The Mekhilta hears four different children, and the Haggadah, read at the seder, names them: the wise one, the wicked one, the simple one, and the one who doesn't know how to ask. Each gets an answer cut to fit. The wise child asks about the laws, and you teach them, all the way to the end. The simple child asks, what is this? and gets one short, true sentence: with a strong hand God brought us out. For the one who can't ask yet, you open the conversation yourself. And the wicked child asks, in Exodus's words, "What mean ye by this service?" Ye, says the Haggadah. You, not us. Here the readers divide. One view takes the Haggadah's words straight: he has stepped outside the family, so the reply is firm. Set his teeth on edge, and say God did this for me. A table needs some lines. The other view, held by some later teachers, notices what the Haggadah doesn't do. It doesn't send him away. He's still counted among the children, still at the table, still owed an answer. One to tell a friend tonight: the four children began with rabbis noticing four verses that didn't match. And both sides agree on this much: no child gets a stock answer.
screen: `FOUR VERSES, FOUR CHILDREN.` · `AN ANSWER CUT TO FIT.` · `YOU, NOT US: A FIRM REPLY.` · `STILL AT THE TABLE.` · then, large: `EVERY CHILD'S ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Pick one person who keeps asking you the same kind of question: a kid, a parent, a partner, a friend. On paper, by hand, write the answer you'd give them, in their words and at their size, not yours. One or two sentences is plenty.
screen: `ONE PERSON, ONE QUESTION.` · `THEIR WORDS, THEIR SIZE.` · `WRITE IT BY HAND.`

segments.voice: Every child's answer: the seder's four children, each owed a reply that fits, even the one who pushes back.
Each child's answer: no stock replies at this table, not even for the one who pushes back. Thirty-nine done.

howItsDone: At the Passover seder, the Haggadah's passage of the four children is read aloud, and some families invite the children at the table to ask their own questions alongside the Four Questions.

fork.setup: your aunt says the sharp answer to the wicked child is mean and should be cut from the seder. what's the strongest case for keeping it?
options: he wrote himself out of 'us', and a table needs some lines, firmly kept.
harsh words are traditional, and tradition should never be questioned.
no child at a real seder is ever wicked, so the answer hurts no one.
fork.reveal: that's the plain reading: 'you, not us' gets a firm reply. the other reading notices he's still at the table, still answered. both read the same paragraph.

original.note: Hebrew: four children (literally four sons), the Haggadah's four askers.

trapdoor: what you thought: four types of kids, ranked from good to bad.
what it means: each child is owed an answer that fits them, even the one who pushes back.
what a scholar hears: the Mekhilta (Bo 18) and the Jerusalem Talmud (Pesachim 10:4) build the four from Exodus 12:26, 13:8, 13:14 and Deuteronomy 6:20; their wording differs from the Haggadah's.

chat.says: my little cousin asked if saba moved because he's dying. my older cousin just smirked. help??
options: Two answers: a short, true, gentle one for the little one; a real talk with the other.
Give them both the same full explanation, so it's fair to each of them.
Answer the little one and ignore the smirk; that one doesn't get a reply.
chat.meaning: The Haggadah's four children each get an answer cut to fit, and even the one who pushes back is still at the table.

notes: Haggadah paraphrased: the four children, 'set his teeth on edge', 'for me, and not for him'; 'with a strong hand' (Exodus 13:14) for the simple child. Confirm.
Exodus 12:26 quoted from JPS 1917 ('What mean ye by this service?'); confirm wording.

Debate: the second view ('he's still counted, still at the table') is attributed to 'some later teachers' without names; a Keeper may wish to name one (e.g. Hasidic and modern readings) or keep it general.

Shape debate: both readings of the wicked child are given in their own terms; the fork asks for the other side's best case. Practice kind: write a line by hand. A parent could use the chat's two-answers idea at dinner.
